newsitem.title: BERMUDA: Canada's Martin rules out early tax cuts.
newsitem.headline: Canada's Martin rules out early tax cuts.

text.p: Canada is not ready to cut taxes despite continued success is reducing the country's budget deficit, Finance Minister Paul Martin said on Wednesday.

"There is no one who would like to bring in a tax cut more than me. But, essentially, Canadians can do the maths as well as anyone else and what that maths says is that...the trend is right (in cutting the deficit), but the battle isn't won," he told Reuters in an interview.

"Canadians don't want us to spend the dividend (of budget savings) until it is there in black and white. This would not be the time for a tax cut," said Martin, in Bermuda for a Commonwealth finance ministers meeting.

Earlier this month, he announced the 1995-96 budget deficit would come in under C$30 billion, but declined to say by how much. The figure would be announced in his budget update sometime in October, he added. Those who advocated tax cuts had to say where they should be. The unemployment insurance premium had already been reduced and would be further cut as the country's financial capacity allowed.
Martin would not speculate on whether the country's future targets to further reduce the budget defici would be exceeded.
"I always knew I was going to be wrong. My goal was to make sure I was wrong on the right side," Martin said, adding that the targets were meant to be the minimum.
He painted a rosy picture of the Canadian economy, saying nearly all the economic indicators, from employment to inflation to the current account, were coming in very well.
"It's hard to be anything but bullish about the Canadian economy," he said.
However, unemployment, even though jobs were being created at a relatively strong pace, remained too high, especially among the young where the focus needed to be.
Domestic demand too was not strong enough, but was on the mend as confidence returns after what he called "stiff medicine" to end a long and deep recession.
"Domestic demand is beginning to come...confidence is building," Martin said. "Now we are in a virtuous circle."
